rows.text: Four successive compacted earthen floors appeared within a 16-square-metre excavation west of the compound. Embedded microdebitage indicates direct blade-production activity on these surfaces.
Operation 17 yielded 406.8 kg of obsidian and 799,384 pieces. Researchers analyzed 329,370 pieces (41.2%); 325,213 in the analyzed sample were core/blade-related artifacts.
In a Room 3 drain-bend cist, excavators identified 16 macrocores, two unused pressure cores, an exhausted-core fragment, 72 bifacial dart points and two knives; they favor dedicatory deposition.
Eighteen AMS radiocarbon determinations include thirteen from floors or work surfaces; many fall around 250–450 CE, whereas two intrusive Mazapan burials yield later ranges.
Researchers classified 95.4% of obsidian visually as green and 4.6% gray. Portable XRF of 409 gray objects attributed 90.5% of that selected subset to Otumba.

At Blockage 11 in TE28 C:East SF20, Sload reports C. Earle Smith identified sedge material with gypsum mineral replacement in a wattle-and-daub fragment examined under magnification; Drewitt also reported plant remains in mud mortar of Blockage 2 south side. Neither directly dates construction nor establishes deliberate sedge addition.

Sload reports 1978 probing every 50 cm at three heights, with lateral depths of 1-3 m beyond modern visible faces and a maximum of 2.95 m south of Station 5. In TE28 Area C, excavation found more than 1 m behind northern stacked facing and 2 m on southern side. Some visible rock walls are ancient and some later INAH consolidation; these readings cannot establish the original cross-section throughout the cave.

Excavation photos captioned in Sload Fig.6.8 depict an overturned stone drain in the mud-mortared interior of Blockage 12 north side and a dressed stone at the ceiling junction within Blockage 3 north side. Original location and ritual use of the worked stones remain unknown.

Carballo reports 22 kg obsidian from 8.1 m3 in 6:N5W1 (2.72 kg/m3) versus 1.7 kg from 13.6 m3 in 22:N5E1 (0.13 kg/m3); obsidian-to-sherd weight ratios 61.7% versus 5.9%. Assemblages were secondary/tertiary mixed refuse, not intact knapping floors.

A polished bone tip was excavated from Deposit 3, Trench 8 Unit R; Carballo describes this as the sole pressure tool within three analyzed deposits. Deposit 3 was mixed secondary lithic refuse, not intact manufacturing floor.
A roof-adornment fragment recovered between Structures 6B and 6E retained red stucco and a trapeze-and-ray/Year Sign motif; a thicker stone variety is reported for the same complex.
The expansion associated with Axayácatl (1469–1481) includes sculpted serpent heads, an Altar of Frogs on Tláloc's north side, and a Coyolxauhqui replica at Huitzilopochtli's south stair.
The earliest excavated temple phase preserves colored walls at Tláloc's shrine and a painted Chac-Mool near its entrance; the Huitzilopochtli side includes a téchcatl ritual stone.

The Casa de las Águilas was built and enlarged three times during c.1430–1500; three rooms are visible, others lie beneath Justo Sierra Street. Interior benches bear processions and two ceramic eagle-warrior figures were found there.
Several superimposed floor surfaces in the north patio are associated by INAH with subsidence and flooding. Phase VI Building B, the tzompantli altar, is decorated with stone-carved human skulls.
A brick drain installed around 1900 beneath present Guatemala Street sliced across Templo Mayor's successive building phases in a strip about two metres wide.
Utility workers exposed the Coyolxauhqui stone at Argentina and Guatemala on 21 February 1978, leading to Proyecto Templo Mayor; the museum opened in 1987.
Four cathedral-atrial archaeological windows show walls tentatively assigned to side chapels and sacristy of a 1525 church commissioned by Cortés, likely completed c.1532 and demolished in 1626.
The 4.0 × 2.2 m atrium window displays colonial tezontle-and-mud masonry with lime-sand plaster and red paint; beneath lie walls and a possibly Mexica flagstone floor.
Excavations during 1975–76 underpinning exposed two phases of a north talud wall assigned to the Mexica Templo del Sol. Tezontle and andesite were mud-set beneath lime-sand-volcanic aggregate stucco.
The second Sagrario window exposes a painted solar-disk pink-andesite plaque with four chalchihuite corner designs, beside wooden foundation piles of the 1749–1768 Sagrario.

A 12 × 4 m archaeological window at the Second Patio Mariano reveals three construction phases of a pre-Hispanic stair, with five andesite-block steps in the latest phase and earlier basalt-slab foundations.
A 3.5 × 1.6 m window excavated in 2003–2004 contains a balustraded stair linking plaza to Mexica shrine. Attribution to a Tezcatlipoca complex remains a hypothesis.

A 6 × 4 m Palace excavation exposes pre-Hispanic stair, ceramic-tube drains, stone pavement and cruciform column support, plus later tezontle drain; the column's association with Cortés's residence is interpretive.

Cortés occupied the former Casas Nuevas of Moctezuma after conquest; his heirs sold the property to the Crown in 1562 for viceregal and Audiencia use; after independence in 1821 the site became Palacio Nacional.
1591 viceregal order charged two Indigenous alcaldes to protect second Chapultepec aqueduct, paid from caja de comunidad.

Public fountain and paid water distribution required traders in San Juan Moyotlan to carry water approximately an extra 1.5km before the new market fountain; Mundy documents water transport by canoe and mule.
Chimalpahin and Codex Aubin record completion of San Juan aqueduct/fountain in 1582; Chimalpahin gives December 31 whereas Aubin translation has an inconsistent December day.
Mundy interprets Codex Aubin water signs with white-edged blue bands as plaster-lined aqueduct, unlike unlined navigable canals; year signs connect work to Valeriano government in 1575 and 1582.
Antonio Valeriano governed Indigenous Mexico-Tenochtitlan from 1573 to 1599 and had taught at Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco, per Mundy citing 1554 Cervantes de Salazar.
Sixteenth-century Uppsala city map depicts water reservoir at Tlatelolco market; Codex Tlatelolco year 1555 depicts possible bird fountain; not proven the same fountain.
Anales de Tlatelolco survives in BNF ms22 on 21 amate leaves and later ms22bis with added or variant material; copy of Rulers List likely seventeenth century.
Tlatelolco Rulers List claims Cuauhtemoc accession 1515, contradicting other Tlatelolco and Florentine Codex accounts naming Itzquauhtzin; treat as contested political memory.
Florentine Codex XII remembers Temilotzin resisting Spanish-Xochimilca forces with Coyohuehuetzin and wielding captured sword; Book VIII associates him with restoration of Tlatelolco governance.
Florentine XII remembers Ecatzin as Tlatelolca commander; captured-banner mention appears only in later Anales ms22bis, not earlier ms22.
Nahua Rulers List says Cuauhtemoc, Coanacoc and Tetlepanquetza hanged at Acalan without inquiry; Spanish accounts differ on conspiracy and whether two or three leaders executed.

In a 29 April 1692 consultation, viceregal authorities allowed broad trading in maize and wheat while trying to secure maize already arranged from Celaya, Toluca and Chalco; Sigüenza later described late-May shortages when the expected shipments lagged.

At about 6:30 p.m. on 8 June, eyewitness Sigüenza says Indigenous women supplied stones to people attacking the viceregal palace; his account also describes participants including Indigenous people, Black and mixed-ancestry residents.
Exbalin reconstructs protesters seeking the corregidor, then the archbishop, and finally the viceroy before destructive attacks on the buildings around the central plaza.

The cabildo abstract dated 16 June 1692 records damage from the 8 June uprising and orders repair of the Alhóndiga, temporary use of the pósito room for council meetings, and return of capitular books held by Sigüenza.
A 26 June 1692 council abstract records councilor Juan de Aguirre's report that, on viceregal orders, he obtained and forwarded thirteen canoes of maize from Chalco to Mexico City.

On 27 June 1692, the city council proposed allocating a share of daily maize deliveries to governors of San Juan and Santiago and other neighborhood leaders to distribute to Indigenous families alongside parish ministers.

A 26 June council proposal sought two rows of lime-and-stone vaulted market stalls with iron-faced doors around Plaza Mayor; a 4 July abstract reports viceregal approval and instruction to master builder Cristóbal de Molina Vargas to draft the plan.

On 11 July 1692 the council recorded Sigüenza's delivery of rescued royal and viceregal portraits and books; Antonio de Ocaña and two colleagues were assigned a total of 18 pesos for helping save documents.

Exbalin reports that on 9 June the viceroy organized a review of Spanish militia and subsequently two cavalry units and two Black and mulatto militia companies, while reforming the palace halberdiers.

Exbalin reports an investigation launched 11 June; within twenty days about eighty accused people faced the Audiencia criminal chamber; twelve death sentences, thirty-two sentences of forced labor and flogging, and nine flogging-only sentences are reported.

After the riot the viceregal government reissued restrictions on Indigenous residence inside the Spanish traza, granting a twenty-day departure period and threatening severe penalties; Exbalin explicitly states the actual degree of enforcement remains unknown.

Exbalin documents a pulque ban dated 19 July 1692, partial relaxation to medicinal white pulque on 31 July and renewed legalization in June 1697, connecting regulatory shifts partly to tax revenues and naval funding.
24 Oct 1985 First Forum and Coordinadora Única de Damnificados formed at Auditorio 5 de Mayo in Nonoalco-Tlatelolco
26 Oct 1985 petition says representatives of 28 neighborhood and earthquake-victim organizations met in Tlatelolco

27 Sep 1985 residents of Morelos, Tepito, Guerrero, Valle Gómez, Tlatelolco and Multifamiliar Juárez attempted to reach president at Los Pinos about emergency response and eviction fears (as reported by Massolo)
Sindicato Nacional de Costureras 19 de Septiembre organized on 20 Oct 1985 on San Antonio Abad, per Massolo
11 Oct 1985 decree expropriated designated damaged properties in Cuauhtémoc, Venustiano Carranza, Benito Juárez and Gustavo A. Madero (decree original not inspected)
14 Oct 1985 emergence of Renovación Habitacional Popular governmental body and program (formal relationship still requires decree)
CUD demanded social housing, residence rights, collective affordable loans, rent control and halt to evictions; demands not achieved outcomes
CUD requested independent and geotechnical structural assessments, including soil mechanics, geology, geophysics and construction elements
Colonia Roma's Unión de Vecinos y Damnificados 19 de Septiembre was established 5 Oct 1985 with claimed representation of 289 buildings, reported by Massolo
Contemporary preliminary report counted 5,728 damaged properties of which 3,745 residential; 47% minor, 38% structural, 15% partial/total collapse, not final census
CUD demanded work cooperatives, unemployment insurance, reinstatement and sanctions for labor exploitation in the garment industry, not proof of enforcement
CUD petition requested civic-leader protection against repression, local decision making and debt-service moratorium for reconstruction funding
